Urinary catheter. Insertion, maintenance and removal, step by step.

Step one. Know the rules. A physician's order is needed for insertion and for removal. Only physicians catheterise children. Female staff catheterise females, and male staff catheterise males. Know when a doctor must catheterise a male patient.
Step two. Choose the right catheter for the purpose: indwelling or intermittent, silicone or latex silicone. Be ready to explain why.
Step three. Prepare. Verify the order, assemble all equipment, explain the procedure, and ensure privacy and good light.
Step four. Critical point. Keep strict asepsis throughout. Your dominant hand is sterile, and your non-dominant hand is clean. Only the sterile hand touches the catheter.
Step five. Before insertion, inflate the balloon with sterile water, check it does not leak, then deflate it fully.
Step six. Critical point. Insert gently until urine flows. If you feel resistance, stop. Never force a catheter. Inflate the balloon according to the manufacturer's instructions.
Step seven. Critical point. Keep all tube ends sterile while connecting. Maintain a closed system, and never disconnect the bag.
Step eight. Secure the catheter to the patient's leg with an approved device, leaving a little slack.
Step nine. Keep the bag below the level of the bladder, to prevent backflow, and always off the floor, to reduce infection risk.
Step ten. Observe the urine: amount, colour, clarity and odour, and check the meatus. Encourage fluids, unless the patient is fluid restricted.

Step eleven. For removal, verify the order and get verbal consent. Deflate the balloon fully. If it will not deflate, do not pull. Follow policy and inform the doctor. Remove gently, and discard the catheter and bag correctly.
Step twelve. After removal, record the time and amount of the first void. If the patient has not voided within eight hours, assess and act as per policy.
Step thirteen. Critical point. For infants, place the baby supine with the thighs abducted, in a frog-leg position, and clean the area with the recommended solution.
Step fourteen. Respect dignity and privacy, reassure the patient with clear explanations, and stay accountable for asepsis and safety.
Step fifteen. Document accurately: urine output, times, the patient's response, urine characteristics, and routine care. Tell the physician about any deviation.
Watch, take the quiz, then get signed off.
